facts.statement: Held the Canadian federal forestry office in the period 1899–1907.
Down the Mackenzie and Up the Yukon in 1906 bears the author’s name and former forestry title; accessible second-edition title page is dated 1913.
Preface states the narrative grew from a government report dated 16 November 1906; includes photographs, many taken by Stewart from steamers.

uncertainties.decision: Accessible Gutenberg witness is a 1913 second edition; cited as such. No assertion that it is the first-edition witness used in production.

en.tagline: Northern rivers seen from the deck of a steamer.
en.intro: A river journey reveals a country in succession: a landing, a settlement, a reach of water, another departure. Stewart follows that changing view through northern Canada, with a forester’s attention to land and resources.
en.orientation: Stewart belongs beside the camping writers through his subject rather than a documented membership of their circle. His northern journey adds transport, forestry and settlement to the world of camp and trail.
origin: Elihu Stewart lived from 1844 to 1935. He held Canada’s federal forestry office in the years 1899–1907; his book identifies him as formerly Superintendent of Forestry for Canada.
career: In the preface to Down the Mackenzie and Up the Yukon in 1906, Stewart explains that the narrative grew from a report submitted to the Canadian government on 16 November 1906. The book allowed room for experiences beyond an official report.
literature: The accessible 1913 second edition joins the river narrative to photographs and a map. Stewart notes that many photographs were taken from steamers. The moving viewpoint is part of the book’s character: places emerge along a route rather than as isolated scenes.

Read beside Seton’s The Arctic Prairies, it offers a different northern journey: an account shaped by waterways and a forestry official’s interests. This is a thematic comparison, not evidence of an encounter.
en.legacy: The book preserves a way of travelling in which rivers joined distant communities. Reading the route today brings attention back to connections between transport, land and the practical knowledge of a journey.
en.bridge: Down the Mackenzie and Up the Yukon in 1906 follows a northern route by its rivers, landings and settlements.
